results.content: • The interviewed teachers revealed that the ‘best’ teaching practices for the 21st century learner are those teaching practices that have student-centered approach. The research literature gives informa-tion on the characteristics of the 21st century learner and the possible teaching practices that can engage such a learner; these include teaching methods that foster teacher-student partnerships in learning, use of technology and en-gagement with deep learning tasks. These findings concur with Knapper (2008) indicating that the best ideas for effective teaching include: teaching methods that focus on the student activity and task performance rather than just acquisition of facts; opportunities for meaningful personal interaction between students and teachers; opportunities for collaborative team learning; more authentic methods of assessment that stress task performance in natural-istic situations, preferably including elements of peer and self-assessment; making learning processes more explicit and encouraging the students to re-flect on the way they learn; learning tasks that encourage integration of infor-mation and skills from different fields.

results.title: Student testing for the 21st century: finding alternatives to forced choice | The Lens
results.content: # Student testing for the 21st century: finding alternatives to forced choice. During one of our regular upper-school team meetings, Dr. Hood asked the group what kind of assessments we used. “Why is that?” Dr. Hood asked. The kids seem to really enjoy them.”. “And, what exactly are you *testing*?”. “I see,” said Dr. Hood. “You do realize that crossword puzzles are a type of forced choice, one of the least effective forms of assessment.”. The others include essays, short written responses, oral reports, performance tasks, teacher observations, and self-assessments. For example, forced choice is OK for testing a student’s grasp of facts, but less so for evaluating her grasp of a process for analyzing a topic. Marzano claims that student self-assessments and performance tasks are the most effective overall, and that forced choice is the least. Yet today (as in the past), the majority of assessments used in schools are forced choice. As for summative assessments, they come in a variety pack that includes various forms of fill-in-the-blank, true-or-false, matching, and the ubiquitous multiple-choice test. 1. If they are not all that effective, why are forced-choice assessments so prevalent? Tests that use forced-choice questions are easy to create and easy to grade. Using various programs (there are several for creating crossword puzzles by the way), teachers can generate a test with a simple keystroke; and they can process test results for an entire classroom in a matter of minutes. Most standardized tests, from the ACT to the GRE, are predominantly forced-choice. Finally, as my “teachable moment” with Dr. Hood would attest, young teachers don’t always have the bandwidth to create and used effective alternative assessments. Testing companies like Pearson and Microsoft are developing resources to support the use of alternative assessments that are easy, accurate and reliable. Edutopia and The Buck Institute for Education are among institutions that push “best practices,”  including teaching and learning experiences built around specific real-world projects and problems. To “prove themselves,” teachers and administrators had to get students to pass a battery of tests in core subject areas.\* So, they did pre- and post-testing for every lesson. As educators like to say, “What gets measured gets taught.”.
